name: Nafsan
confidence_why: Thieberger's 2006 grammar describes initial stress by ear, but Early (2007) heard final stress on the grammar's own recordings, and the instrumental studies of Billington, Fletcher, Thieberger and Volchok (2018, 2020) and Billington, Thieberger and Fletcher (2020, 2023), with the grammar's author among them, find consistently higher pitch on the final syllable and no sign of initial prominence, while leaving open whether this right-edge prominence is word stress or a phrase-level accent.

Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53(2): 511–531. doi:10.1017/S0025100321000177 (CC BY Minerva Access copy). Conflicting primary: Thieberger, Nicholas. 2006. A Grammar of South Efate: An Oceanic Language of Vanuatu. Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 33. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press, §3.5.4 Stress, pp. 65–66; §3.6.1.2, p. 69 (Minerva Access copy).
catalog_locator: JIPA 2023, 'Prosody' section, FirstView pp. 17–18. Thieberger 2006 §3.5.4 pp. 65–66; §3.6.1.2 p. 69.
catalog_quote: Research on the prosodic characteristics of Nafsan is ongoing, but indications are that there is a strong preference for words to be more prominent at the right edge. Analyses of disyllabic and trisyllabic words produced in an utterance-medial frame show a clear pattern of higher fundamental frequency values in final compared to preceding syllables (Billington et al. 2018, 2020). Both short and long final vowels can be prominent on the basis of fundamental frequency, and this occurs regardless of whether there is a long vowel in a preceding syllable ... This suggests that syllable weight does not influence the location of prominence within the word. ... Observations on productive patterns of vowel deletion, noted earlier, provide supporting evidence for prominence patterns in that when deletion takes place, it appears to primarily affect penultimate, and thereby pre-tonic, syllables. While previous descriptions of Nafsan have discussed various possible prominence patterns as lexical stress, there is emerging evidence that accentual prominence in Nafsan may be phrasal. Investigations of words of different lengths in initial, medial and final utterance positions and under different focus conditions suggest that strong rising f0 movements at the right edge of a word may demarcate an accentual phrase, and also find that there may be a shift in prominence location under some conditions, for example in non-focal contexts (Fletcher, Billington & Thieberger 2019).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The two first-hand descriptions disagree. The reference grammar (Thieberger 2006: 65–66, saved) says stress is non-contrastive and that initial stress is the dominant pattern for monomorphemic roots, with lexical exceptions (na-initial nouns stressed on the syllable after na-; some plant names penultimate). The instrumental work by the same team (JASA 2020; JIPA Illustration 2023) finds instead a consistent right-edge (word-final) f0 prominence, independent of vowel length/syllable weight, with vowel deletion targeting the pre-tonic penult, and suggests this prominence is a phrasal (accentual-phrase) boundary tone rather than lexical stress. The most recent authoritative description therefore treats the lexical-stress analysis as superseded but leaves the word-level pattern open ('research.. ongoing').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Thieberger 2006: 65–66: words with article na- stress the first syllable following na- (na.'fa.nu 'heaven'); some na- words take initial stress ('na.ta.mol 'person'); multisyllabic plant names show penultimate stress (nau.'?a.las); suffixation re-assigns stress and destresses/deletes medial vowels (p. 69). JIPA 2023 / IJL 2020: prominence location may shift under pragmatic/focus conditions, e.g. in non-focal contexts (Fletcher et al. 2019). Early 2007 review: reviewer heard final stress where the grammar records initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Grammar statement is impressionistic, about citation-form monomorphemic words from recordings. Instrumental results are for di-/trisyllabic words in an utterance-medial carrier frame; the right-edge prominence is argued to be phrasal (accentual phrase boundary tone) rather than word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Nafsan = South Efate (sout2856, ISO erk) as spoken in Erakor (primary), Eratap and Pango villages; Thieberger's corpus and the phonetic studies are Erakor-based. Not to be confused with the 'compromise literary dialect' of Macdonald 1907 or with Efate/North Efate (Nakanamanga, efat1235 / nort2836).

new_statements.quote: These findings provide compelling evidence that disyllabic Nafsan words are more prominent at the right edge. The consistent pattern of higher f0 values in final compared to initial syllables, regardless of the phonemic length of the vowel, suggests that f0 likely plays an important role in prominence marking. […] The results presented here accord with other impressions of final prominence in Nafsan [11, 5], and in pointing towards the importance of f0 as a major correlate, also suggest the possibility that prominence marking in Nafsan is more like that of languages such as Japanese which have been described as having non-stress accent [24].

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing JIPA 2023 statement (right-edge prominence, higher f0 at the final syllable); adds the instrumental detail (f0 the main cue, duration/intensity cue vowel length not position, 1,114 tokens, four speakers, disyllables only) and the explicit hedge that the right-edge f0 rise may be a non-stress accent or phrase-level tone rather than word stress. The catalog record's rule field is empty; this work supports filling it as right-edge/final prominence with the lexical-vs-phrasal status left open.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In disyllabic words (CV.CVC, CV.CVVC, CVV.CVC, CVV.CVVC) recorded in an utterance-medial frame by four Erakor speakers, the final syllable has significantly higher f0 (14–19 Hz) than the initial syllable in every structure, regardless of vowel length; duration and intensity differences track phonemic vowel length, not word position, so they are at most minor prominence cues. The authors conclude that prominence is at the right edge of the word with f0 as the primary correlate. They also note that earlier descriptions proposed both initial stress (Thieberger 2006) and final stress (Capell ms), and they raise the possibility that this right-edge high f0 is a non-stress accent (Japanese-like) or a phrase-edge high tone (Korean/French-like) rather than lexical stress, to be settled by ongoing research. Also p. 137: 'This paper presents preliminary acoustic and durational results for Nafsan … which suggest a preference for prominence at the right edge of words, with fundamental frequency as a primary correlate.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only disyllables were analysed.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Notes that penultimate short vowels in CV syllables show centralisation/reduction (lower F1, F2) even when not deleted, consistent with productive deletion of penultimate short vowels; the one positional duration difference (initial vs final short vowels in CV.CVC, 8 ms) is called very small.
new_statements.identity_note: Billington et al. 2018 recorded four adult first-language speakers of Nafsan from Erakor village (Nafsan = South Efate, spoken in Erakor, Eratap and Pango). Macdonald 1907 was based at Havannah Harbour (north-west Efate) from 1872 and his 'Efatese' is that variety; his accent remark is about Oceanic languages in general. Capell's manuscript covers the Nguna-Efate dialects (not opened).

It is the strong stress that has done much to differentiate the Efate dialects from those of the surrounding islands. The following are the observed facts for Nguna itself: ... 2. Words of two syllables are normally stressed on the first syllable ... [ms p. 9–10, images 12–13] The foregoing remarks apply only to Nguna - Tongoa and Sesake, not to the dialects which permit close syllables, for here the loss of a final vowel may result in a final stressed syllable. new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record for Nafsan has an empty rule; the existing statement (Billington, Thieberger & Fletcher 2023 JIPA) reports a strong preference for right-edge (final) prominence, classed 'unclear or contradictory'. Capell's only Nafsan-relevant remark — that in the closed-syllable Efate dialects, especially Erakor, final-vowel loss 'may result in a final stressed syllable' — is compatible with right-edge prominence and supplies the diachronic mechanism (retained stress on an originally penultimate syllable made final by apocope). It does not state a fixed rule, so it does not resolve the catalog's 'unclear' status; it mildly disfavors Thieberger 2006's 'initial stress is the dominant pattern'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Capell states explicit placement rules only for Nguna (North Efate): stress strong; disyllables stressed on the first syllable; words of three or more syllables 'rather irregular' but frequently initial, with vowel sonority/'weight' influencing placement; reduplications weak stress on 1st + strong on 3rd syllable; inflectional suffixes do not shift stress except the enclitic 3sg object -a, which advances stress one syllable; in Nguna 'no instances of stress on a final syllable appear'. For the Efate dialects that allow closed syllables (Havannah Harbour and Erakor = Nafsan) he explicitly says these Nguna rules do NOT apply: loss of final vowels there 'may result in a final stressed syllable', i.e. the originally stressed (penultimate) syllable becomes word-final after apocope (CVCV > CVC), Erakor being the dialect that drops the most final vowels. No synchronic stress rule for Erakor/Nafsan is stated beyond this.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only for Nguna: reduplications carry a weak stress on the first syllable and strong stress on the third (ˌnaniˈnani 'goat', ˌsoroˈsoro 'tell a lie'); compounds retain original stresses with weakening of the earlier ones. Nothing on secondary stress for Erakor/Nafsan.
new_statements.exceptions: Nguna only: possessive suffixes 'uncertain' (stress sometimes advanced in pause, 'not a regular treatment'); enclitic -a 'him/her/it' advances stress by one syllable; takaˈlapa vs ˈtakariki attributed to vowel sonority ('weight'). For Efate dialects: final stressed syllables arise where a final vowel has been lost.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell's typescript is a comparative sketch of the whole Nguna–Efate dialect chain; its stress rules are stated 'for Nguna itself' (North Efate, Glottolog nort2836, ISO llp) and extended to Tongoa and Sesake. Nafsan appears as 'Erakor' (SW Efate: Pango, Erakor, Eratap; 'the clearest Efate type', ms p. 4) and 'H.H.' is MacDonald's Havannah Harbour dialect (now Lelepa). Only the apocope/final-stress remark and the CVCV > CVC statement concern Erakor.

readall_conflicts: The sources disagree on placement and on whether Nafsan has word stress at all. Impressionistic descriptions put the accent at the left edge: Thieberger 2006 §3.5.4 (initial stress, non-contrastive, stress on the syllable after the article na-) and, generically for 'the Oceanic dialects', Macdonald 1907 p. 51 (accent on the first syllable). The instrumental study Billington et al. 2018 (pp. 137, 140) finds the opposite in disyllables: consistently higher f0 on the final syllable regardless of vowel length, with duration and intensity cueing vowel length rather than position, and states that this accords with earlier impressions of final prominence in Capell's unopened Nguna-Efate ms; this agrees with the existing JIPA 2023 statement of right-edge prominence. Billington et al. 2018 themselves leave open whether the right-edge f0 rise is lexical stress, a Japanese-type non-stress accent, or a Korean/French-type phrase-edge high tone, so even the best-supported placement (right edge) is not asserted as word stress. If a single placement must be chosen the instrumental right-edge evidence outweighs the older impressions. No new hard conflict. Capell's ms gives explicit stress rules only for Nguna (North Efate: initial stress in disyllables, longer words irregular/often initial, never final) and says these do not carry over to the Efate dialects (Havannah Harbour, Erakor = Nafsan), where apocope 'may result in a final stressed syllable'. That remark sides with the right-edge/fina…

sources.note: §3.5.4 Stress, pp. 65–66 (pp. 93–94): 'Stress is not contrastive in South Efate.' Initial stress is the dominant pattern for monomorphemic roots (ex. 35–36a); words with the article na- stress the first syllable after na- (36b), some na- words have initial stress (36c), and a group of multisyllabic plant names has penultimate stress (36d). Suffixation re-assigns stress and destresses/deletes medial vowels (§3.6.1, p. 69).
